activities.caption: which curve is the sorted-array lookup?
activities.name: dsBintrace

config.prompt: Items stored against worst-case comparisons needed — which curve is lookup in a sorted array?
config.why: 1 million items in about 20 comparisons, 1 billion in 30 — the logarithm's superpower, at the price of O(n) insertion into the ordered shelf.

activities.caption: true or false — hash table versus tree
activities.name: dsHashJudge

statements.s: Hash tables are simply faster than balanced trees.
statements.why: It wins lookups on average but cannot return sorted order, degrades under adversarial keys, and pays resizing lumps.

statements.s: A balanced tree's O(log n) is a worst-case guarantee with ordered iteration included.
statements.why: The two things hash tables cannot give — which is why real systems often run both indexes over the same store.

statements.s: If an attacker can choose keys that all collide, the table degrades to O(n) per lookup.
statements.why: The hash-flooding denial-of-service attack — which is why languages seed their hash functions randomly.

statements.s: A heap guarantees O(log n) lookup of any arbitrary element.
statements.why: Only insert/extract-min; lookup of an arbitrary element is O(n) — match the operation list to the structure, not the shape to the slogan.

activities.caption: call the depth for a billion keys
activities.name: dsBtreeEst

config.prompt: A B-tree of order 500 — each node packed with keys sized to one disk block. Roughly how deep must it be to reach a billion keys?
config.why: Depth 4 — each level multiplies by ~500, so a search reads 3–4 pages even for billions of items: the reason database indexes look like this.
config.context: Depth grows by 1 each time capacity squares — the log is the message.

activities.caption: pair each file layout with its RAM counterpart
activities.name: dsFileMatch

config.prompt: Pair each file layout with its counterpart in RAM:

pairs.right: records in order — append cheap, lookup reads past everything earlier: the tape model
seek by record number — the disk analogue of array indexing
sorted key → position table, binary-searched then one direct seek — a B-tree waiting to happen
compact and fast, where text is debuggable and portable

config.why: When data must outlive the program, state the access pattern first and only then pick the layout.

activities.anchor: every node costs an allocation and a pointer's memory
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the linked-list ledger
activities.name: dsMidSpot

config.prompt: A summary of the linked-list ledger contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: A linked list stores nodes with a value and a pointer, so it can live anywhere in memory.
Insertion and removal at a known node are pure pointer surgery — O(1), no shifting.
Doubly linked lists add a back link — O(1) removal given the element, at the price of two links per element.
A sorted linked list supports binary search, because finding the middle is one arithmetic act on an index.
Pointer-chasing defeats the CPU cache, so list traversal runs 10–50× slower than an array walk.
config.correction: Binary search needs O(1) access to the middle — arithmetic on an index, which arrays have and pointers do not; on a list, finding the middle is itself a walk, and the log n collapses to O(n).
config.why: Sorting a list buys order, not halves — the access pattern, not the sortedness, decides what search costs.

activities.anchor: swap with the parent while smaller
activities.caption: build the min-heap state by state
activities.name: dsHeapOrder

config.prompt: Build a min-heap from 5, 3, 8, 1 — put the states in order:
config.why: Insert appends and bubbles up; extract-min moves the last element to the top and bubbles down — log n each way, the priority queue of Dijkstra and the schedulers.

activities.anchor: the hard modelling questions in industry are graph questions
activities.caption: choose the representation, then the traversal
activities.name: dsGraphBranch

config.root: You are handed a scenario the containers do not fit. Walk the representation choice.

start.text: A social network: 100 million users, average 200 friends each. How do you store it?

choices.label: Adjacency list — an array of neighbour lists
choices.feedback: Sparse graph: 100M × 200 ≈ 20 billion entries, not 10,000 trillion — the list is the only sane size.

sparse.text: Sparse wins. And the traversal for 'shortest number of hops between two users'?

choices.label: BFS with a queue — explore in distance layers
choices.feedback: Earlier arrivals processed first is exactly what layer-by-layer shortest-hop search needs.

choices.label: DFS with a stack — dive deep, backtrack
choices.feedback: DFS finds structure and cycles beautifully — but the first path it finds is not the shortest.

dense.text: The matrix suits dense small graphs — constant-time edge tests at quadratic memory cost. At 100 million nodes it is 10 quadrillion cells of mostly zero.

bfs.text: Queue + BFS: distance layers, shortest hops. Stack + DFS: structure and cycles. Same graph, different discipline.

dfs.text: DFS answers 'is there a cycle?', BFS answers 'how many hops?' — pick by question.

config.why: A list is the general structure with one successor; a tree, one parent — and when nothing fits, name the entities and relationships and let it take over.
